A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RewardDS, with matching core methods and experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original QA and code-generation experiments, component ablations, LLM-judge evaluations, hyperparameter analyses, and comparisons across target-model backbones.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds privacy attacks, runtime measurements, filtering comparisons, and additional sensitivity and proxy-model experiments.

M1.justification: The proxy-model training procedure, reward loss, filtering, and iterative refinement remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and all eight prompt templates match across versions. Testing different proxy models does not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: The medical, financial, and code-generation datasets and tasks remain. V2 adds medical-data reconstruction and membership-inference scenarios, involving partial private-text prefixes and augmented nonmember examples (Section 6.4 and Appendix G). These extend evaluation coverage without adding another domain.

E2.justification: The main benchmark and target-backbone comparator sets remain unchanged. V2 adds a No Protection control to the attack evaluation and explicit reward-based filtering controls in Table 4. Its revised case study also compares RewardDS directly with DP-Generation, DP-Instruct, and KnowledgeSG.

E3.justification: Reported medical training/synthetic sample counts change from 3,364/6,728 to 3,210/6,420, while development and test counts remain fixed (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 7). V2 substantially expands evaluation protocols through privacy attacks, varying total privacy budgets and synthetic-data quantities, alternative proxy configurations, and cost measurements. The count revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds privacy attacks, refinement-stage downstream evaluation, cost profiling, filtering-only comparisons, data-quantity and privacy-budget sensitivity, and proxy-model heterogeneity/scale analyses. The case study becomes a baseline-response comparison. V1's financial/code reward-distribution panels disappear, while existing target-backbone and k/N analyses are retained and reorganized.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results in Tables 2–6 and Figures 4–6, including 448 minutes for RewardDS versus 315 for DP-Generation and new attack, filtering, sensitivity, and proxy-model outcomes. Table 1 and the retained target-backbone table keep their numerical entries despite revised medical sample counts. The case-study responses change, and the financial hyperparameter plots change their R1/RL series attribution.

T1.justification: Equation 1, Algorithm 1, and Section 5's DP post-processing and sequential-composition argument remain unchanged, including the total budget of (2ε, 2δ). No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims: reward-driven synthetic-data improvement through Reward Guided Filtering and Self-Optimizing Refinement for privacy-preserving fine-tuning. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: V2 introduces explanations linking attack resistance to divided privacy budgets, proxy performance to model compatibility and reward-model capacity, and scarce-data performance to refinement. It presents measured overhead as minimal and removes the limitations paragraph explicitly emphasizing additional reward-model training cost. These substantially expand and change the paper's interpretation of effectiveness and practicality.

D1.justification: Appendix G newly documents attack construction, 10-token prefixes, greedy decoding, and a 256-token output limit. V2 also supplies runtime information and a promised code/data repository location. Core training, hardware, and prompt details remain; the baseline appendix loses v1's detailed DP-Instruct clustering/histogram and KnowledgeSG BLEU-filter descriptions, without establishing implementation changes.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A recast related work into anonymity-, encryption-, and synthesis-based approaches. V2 adds substantive discussion of encryption methods, including Lou, Frery, and You, alongside Hou and privacy-attack references. Earlier discussions of API-based generation and multi-model synthesis are removed, materially changing the research positioning.

P1.justification: Related work, the experimental narrative, and the appendices are substantially reorganized. LLM-judge discussion moves into Main Results and Appendix E; medical k/N and privacy-allocation analyses move to appendices; an appendix overview is added. Baseline, case-study, and limitations prose is rewritten, although the core method text remains largely stable.

P2.justification: V2 introduces five new tables, privacy and budget plots, a redesigned Figure 5, and an expanded multi-method Figure 7. Figure 1 is redrawn and relocated, Figure 3 is reduced in size, and existing hyperparameter displays are relocated and split. The financial-QA plots also change their metric-to-series mapping.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method. Privacy attacks and filtering-only comparisons address central evidence gaps in v1, while cost and sensitivity analyses make practical tradeoffs more assessable. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including the unexplained medical-count revision with unchanged headline scores, labeling 642 of 6,420 samples as 1%, and using parameter counts as a GPU-memory proxy.
